# Results {#sec-results}

```{python}
#| include: false
# inbound from _04: reg, df, model, model_log, X_ml, X_test, y_test, y_pred_rf,
# best_rf, perm_imp, joint_drop, year_drop, state_drop, engine,
# ols_log_test_r2, rf_log_test_r2, nn_test_r2,
# ols_log_test_mae, rf_log_test_mae, nn_test_mae
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
from great_tables import GT

res_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share",
          "poverty_rate","unemployment_rate","log_population"]

mean_pp=float(reg["affordability_salary"].mean())
group_terms=["non_routine_manual_share","routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share"]
group_names=["Non-Routine Manual","Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual"]
```

The analysis supports four findings. The balance of work in a county is associated with its purchasing power, and the association survives controls for poverty, unemployment, time, and geography. The relationship is proportional rather than linear in dollars, so the flexible models cannot improve on the log linear fit. Poverty rate remains the single strongest correlate of purchasing power throughout, with the task groups adding real signal beyond it. And the task group differences behind the association are durable features of places, so the purchasing power gaps they carry are durable too. The subsections below work through these findings, and through the geography and the model behavior behind them.

## The association

```{python}
#| include: false
# log specification coefficients (model_log fit in _04, cluster robust), expressed as
# dollars at the panel mean per one percentage point shift
coef_rows=[]
for term, name in zip(group_terms, group_names):
    b=model_log.params[term]
    se=model_log.bse[term]
    est=(np.exp(b*0.01)-1)*mean_pp
    lo=(np.exp((b-1.96*se)*0.01)-1)*mean_pp
    hi=(np.exp((b+1.96*se)*0.01)-1)*mean_pp
    coef_rows.append({"group":name, "est":est, "lo":lo, "hi":hi})
coef_df=pd.DataFrame(coef_rows)
```

The log specification of the panel regression is the model we use for inference, for the diagnostic reasons set out in @sec-analysis. @fig-coefplot reports its task group coefficients as the change in purchasing power, in dollars at the panel mean, associated with a one percentage point shift into each group and out of non-routine cognitive work, the reference group. A one percentage point shift toward non-routine manual work is associated with roughly \$846 less in purchasing power, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus \$38, evaluated at the panel mean. Routine cognitive and routine manual shifts carry smaller but clearly negative associations, and the ordering matches the level specification reported in @sec-analysis. For scale, each additional percentage point of poverty rate is associated with roughly 2.9 percent lower purchasing power, a larger proportional difference than any single task group carries.

```{python}
#| label: fig-coefplot
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Task group coefficients from the log specification of the panel regression, expressed as dollars of purchasing power at the panel mean per one percentage point shift into each group, with 95 percent intervals. Non-routine cognitive is the reference group at zero. Standard errors are clustered by county."
%%R -i coef_df -w 8 -h 3.5 -u in -r 150
coef_df$group <- factor(coef_df$group,
    levels=rev(c("Non-Routine Manual","Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual")))

dollar_axis <- function(v) {
  ifelse(is.na(v), "",
    ifelse(v == 0, "$0",
      sprintf("%s$%s", ifelse(v < 0, "-", ""),
              formatC(abs(v), format="d", big.mark=","))))
}

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x=est, y=group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed", linewidth=0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin=lo, xmax=hi), orientation="y", width=0.15, color="#0072B2") +
  geom_point(size=2.6, color="#0072B2") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels=dollar_axis) +
  labs(x="Change in Purchasing Power per Percentage Point Shift ($ at Panel Mean)", y=NULL)
```

## Not poverty in disguise

A natural objection is that the task groups merely proxy for poverty, since poor counties hold more routine work. @fig-coefcompare tests that directly by fitting the level panel regression twice on the same rows, once with task groups and year indicators only, and once adding poverty rate, unemployment rate, and log population, the specification reported in @sec-analysis. The associations shrink when the controls enter, which is what we would expect, since poverty absorbs shared variation. All three remain large, negative, and precisely estimated. The task group association is smaller than it first appears and clearly real.

```{python}
#| include: false
share_terms=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share"]

X_nocontrols=pd.concat([reg[share_terms],
                        pd.get_dummies(reg["year"], prefix="year", drop_first=True).astype(float)], axis=1)
X_nocontrols=sm.add_constant(X_nocontrols)
model_nc=sm.OLS(reg["affordability_salary"], X_nocontrols).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})

compare_rows=[]
for term, name in zip(share_terms, ["Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual","Non-Routine Manual"]):
    for m, spec in [(model_nc, "Task Groups and Year Only"), (model, "With Controls")]:
        b=m.params[term]/100
        se=m.bse[term]/100
        compare_rows.append({"group":name, "spec":spec, "est":b,
                             "lo":b-1.96*se, "hi":b+1.96*se})
compare_df=pd.DataFrame(compare_rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-coefcompare
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Task group coefficients from the level panel regression before and after adding poverty, unemployment, and population controls, in dollars per one percentage point shift, with 95 percent intervals. The associations shrink with controls but remain large, negative, and precisely estimated."
%%R -i compare_df -w 9 -h 4 -u in -r 150
compare_df$group <- factor(compare_df$group,
    levels=rev(c("Non-Routine Manual","Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual")))
compare_df$spec <- factor(compare_df$spec,
    levels=c("Task Groups and Year Only","With Controls"))

dollar_axis <- function(v) {
  ifelse(is.na(v), "",
    ifelse(v == 0, "$0",
      sprintf("%s$%s", ifelse(v < 0, "-", ""),
              formatC(abs(v), format="d", big.mark=","))))
}

ggplot(compare_df, aes(x=est, y=group, color=spec)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed", linewidth=0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin=lo, xmax=hi), orientation="y", width=0.2,
                position=position_dodge(width=0.5)) +
  geom_point(size=2.2, position=position_dodge(width=0.5)) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Task Groups and Year Only"="grey55",
                              "With Controls"="#0072B2")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels=dollar_axis) +
  labs(x="Change in Purchasing Power per Percentage Point Shift ($)", y=NULL, color=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

## Where purchasing power is strained

The association has a geography. @fig-afford-map maps mean purchasing power by county across the study period, on the full set of counties with a purchasing power value rather than the analytical panel alone, since the outcome requires only income and a price parity. Purchasing power runs highest across the metropolitan Northeast corridor, the upper Midwest, and pockets of the mountain West, and lowest across the rural South and the southern border region, the same regions where routine intensive work concentrates. The map shows the outcome side of the association the coefficients estimate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-afford-map
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean purchasing power by county, 2008 to 2023, in dollars at national average prices. The color range is clipped at the 2nd and 98th percentiles so extreme counties do not compress the scale. Counties without a purchasing power value are shown in gray. Continental United States only."
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

map_all=pd.read_sql("""
    select county_fips, avg(affordability_salary) as purchasing_power
    from county_affordability
    group by county_fips
""", engine)
map_all['fips']=map_all['county_fips'].astype(str).str.zfill(5)

gdf_map=gpd.read_file("https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2021/shp/cb_2021_us_county_500k.zip")
gdf_map=gdf_map.rename(columns={'GEOID':'fips'})

vmin=map_all['purchasing_power'].quantile(0.02)
vmax=map_all['purchasing_power'].quantile(0.98)

merged_map=gdf_map.merge(map_all[['fips','purchasing_power']], on='fips', how='left')
merged_map=merged_map[~merged_map['STATEFP'].isin(['02','15','60','66','69','72','78'])]

fig, ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(12,7))
merged_map.plot(column='purchasing_power', cmap='viridis', vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax,
                linewidth=0.1, edgecolor='white', ax=ax,
                legend=True,
                legend_kwds={'label':'mean purchasing power ($)',
                    'orientation':'horizontal', 'shrink':0.3, 'pad':0.02, 'aspect':35},
                missing_kwds={'color':'#eeeeee'})
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

## The relationship is proportional

@sec-analysis climbed the model complexity ladder and reported where each rung landed. @fig-modelcomp collects the ending, held out R² on the dollar scale for the three models scored on the same held out counties. The log target linear model and the random forest land at the same level, statistically indistinguishable under the grouped cross validation in @sec-analysis, and the neural network trails both. @tbl-modelmetrics adds mean absolute error, where the linear model's typical prediction is off by a few hundred dollars less than the forest's.

```{python}
#| include: false
modelcomp_df=pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["OLS (Log Target)","Random Forest (Log Target)","Neural Network"],
    "r2": [ols_log_test_r2, rf_log_test_r2, nn_test_r2],
})
comp_ymin=float(min(0, modelcomp_df["r2"].min()*1.15))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-modelcomp
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Held out R-squared on the dollar scale for the three models, each scored on the same held out counties from the grouped split. The log target linear model and the random forest are statistically indistinguishable, and the neural network trails both, so added model complexity finds no signal the log linear fit misses."
%%R -i modelcomp_df -i comp_ymin -w 8 -h 3.5 -u in -r 150
modelcomp_df$model <- factor(modelcomp_df$model,
    levels=c("OLS (Log Target)","Random Forest (Log Target)","Neural Network"))

ggplot(modelcomp_df, aes(x=model, y=r2, fill=model)) +
  geom_col(width=0.55, show.legend=FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label=sprintf("%.3f", r2)), vjust=-0.5, size=3.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("OLS (Log Target)"="#009E73",
                             "Random Forest (Log Target)"="#CC79A7",
                             "Neural Network"="grey60")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(comp_ymin, 1)) +
  labs(x=NULL, y="Held Out R Squared ($ Scale)")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-modelmetrics
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Held out performance on the same held out counties, dollar scale."

metrics_df=pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["OLS (log target)","Random forest (log target)","Neural network"],
    "Held out R squared": [ols_log_test_r2, rf_log_test_r2, nn_test_r2],
    "Mean absolute error ($)": [ols_log_test_mae, rf_log_test_mae, nn_test_mae],
})

(GT(metrics_df)
  .fmt_number(columns="Held out R squared", decimals=3)
  .fmt_currency(columns="Mean absolute error ($)", decimals=0)
  .tab_source_note("All models scored on the identical held out counties from the grouped split."))
```

This is the ladder's stopping rule working as designed. A random forest can represent any interaction or curvature the data contain, and it finds nothing beyond what the log transformation already captured. The binned comparison in @fig-binned shows the same conclusion in the units of the outcome. Across bins of routine cognitive work, the forest's predictions track actual purchasing power closely, and both trace the smooth, monotonic pattern a proportional relationship implies. The association between the balance of work and purchasing power is real, and it is not exotic.

```{python}
#| include: false
binned_ml=pd.DataFrame({
    "rc": X_test["routine_cognitive_share"].values,
    "Actual": y_test.values,
    "Random Forest": y_pred_rf,
})
binned_ml["bin"]=pd.qcut(binned_ml["rc"], 10, labels=False)
binned_means=binned_ml.groupby("bin")[["rc","Actual","Random Forest"]].mean().reset_index(drop=True)
binned_long=binned_means.melt(id_vars="rc", value_vars=["Actual","Random Forest"],
                              var_name="series", value_name="pp")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-binned
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean actual and random forest predicted purchasing power across ten equal count bins of routine cognitive work, on the held out test counties. The forest tracks the actual pattern closely, and both decline smoothly as routine cognitive work rises."
%%R -i binned_long -w 8 -h 4 -u in -r 150
ggplot(binned_long, aes(x=rc, y=pp, color=series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=0.7) +
  geom_point(size=2) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Actual"="#0072B2","Random Forest"="#CC79A7")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=function(v) sprintf("$%s", formatC(round(v), format="d", big.mark=","))) +
  labs(x="Routine Cognitive Group Value (Bin Mean)", y="Mean Purchasing Power", color=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

## What carries the signal

@fig-importance ranks what the random forest relies on, using the grouped permutation approach from @sec-analysis so that indicator blocks and the task groups are each scored as a unit. Poverty rate carries the largest single drop, consistent with its dominance in the regression. The four task groups together come next at 0.153, ahead of the year block at 0.128, and state adds almost nothing at 0.008 once everything else is present. The task groups matter as a set, which is what a set of parts of a whole should do.

```{python}
#| include: false
pov_idx=list(X_test.columns).index("poverty_rate")
unemp_idx=list(X_test.columns).index("unemployment_rate")

importance_df=pd.DataFrame({
    "feature": ["Poverty Rate","Task Groups (Joint)","Year (Joint)",
                "Unemployment Rate","State (Joint)"],
    "drop": [perm_imp.importances_mean[pov_idx], joint_drop, year_drop,
             perm_imp.importances_mean[unemp_idx], state_drop],
}).sort_values("drop")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-importance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Feature importance from grouped permutation on the held out test counties, measured as the drop in R-squared when each feature or block is shuffled. The task groups are permuted jointly, as are the year and state indicator blocks. Larger drops indicate features the model relies on more."
%%R -i importance_df -w 8 -h 3.5 -u in -r 150
importance_df$feature <- factor(importance_df$feature, levels=importance_df$feature)

ggplot(importance_df, aes(x=drop, y=feature)) +
  geom_col(width=0.6, fill="#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label=sprintf("%.3f", drop)), hjust=-0.2, size=3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand=expansion(mult=c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x="Drop in Held Out R Squared When Permuted", y=NULL)
```

@fig-pdp completes the picture with the forest's partial dependence on the three non reference task groups. Each curve shows predicted purchasing power as one group's value moves across its observed range with all other features held at their values. The curves decline smoothly and near monotonically, with no thresholds or reversals, which is the shape a proportional association implies and the reason the flexible model could not beat the log linear one.

```{python}
#| include: false
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence

pdp_frames=[]
for term, name in zip(["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share"],
                      ["Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual","Non-Routine Manual"]):
    pd_res=partial_dependence(best_rf, X_test, [term], kind="average", grid_resolution=40)
    grid=pd_res["grid_values"][0] if "grid_values" in pd_res else pd_res["values"][0]
    pdp_frames.append(pd.DataFrame({"x":grid,
                                    "y":pd_res["average"][0],
                                    "group":name}))
pdp_df=pd.concat(pdp_frames, ignore_index=True)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pdp
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Random forest partial dependence of predicted purchasing power on each non reference task group, computed on the held out test counties. Each curve moves one group across its observed range with all other features held at their values. The smooth, near monotonic declines match a proportional association."
%%R -i pdp_df -w 10 -h 3.5 -u in -r 150
ggplot(pdp_df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_line(color="#CC79A7", linewidth=0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales="free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=function(v) sprintf("$%s", formatC(round(v), format="d", big.mark=","))) +
  labs(x="Task Group Value", y="Predicted Purchasing Power")
```

## The differences are durable

The final question is whether these associations describe a stable feature of places or a moment in time. Three pieces of evidence say stable. @fig-taskarea shows the national balance across the four task groups over the panel, which moves little across fifteen years apart from the 2009 to 2010 step produced by the Census occupation coding change described in @sec-data.

```{python}
#| include: false
area_df=(df.groupby("year")[["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share",
                             "non_routine_cognitive_share","non_routine_manual_share"]]
           .mean().reset_index()
           .melt(id_vars="year", var_name="group", value_name="share"))
area_names={"routine_cognitive_share":"Routine Cognitive",
            "routine_manual_share":"Routine Manual",
            "non_routine_cognitive_share":"Non-Routine Cognitive",
            "non_routine_manual_share":"Non-Routine Manual"}
area_df["group"]=area_df["group"].map(area_names)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-taskarea
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean task group values across panel counties by year. The balance across the four groups is nearly constant over the study period. The visible step between 2009 and 2010 reflects the Census occupation coding change, and 2020 is absent because ACS published no 1 year estimates that year."
%%R -i area_df -w 9 -h 4 -u in -r 150
area_df$group <- factor(area_df$group,
    levels=c("Non-Routine Cognitive","Non-Routine Manual",
             "Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual"))

ggplot(area_df, aes(x=year, y=share, fill=group)) +
  geom_area(alpha=0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Non-Routine Cognitive"="#0072B2",
                             "Non-Routine Manual"="#CC79A7",
                             "Routine Cognitive"="#009E73",
                             "Routine Manual"="#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=function(v) sprintf("%.0f%%", v*100)) +
  labs(x="Year", y="Mean Group Value Across Counties", fill=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

Individual counties hold their positions as well, not just the national aggregate. @tbl-rankcorr reports the rank correlation of each group's county ordering between 2010 and 2023, computed from 2010 onward to step over the coding change. Routine manual and non-routine cognitive hold their orderings most strongly, so the counties with the most of each in 2010 are largely the same counties in 2023. Non-routine manual is more mobile, and routine cognitive reorders the most, which is consistent with it being the one group carrying substantial within county movement in the variance decomposition of @sec-analysis.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rankcorr
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Spearman rank correlation of county orderings between 2010 and 2023, by task group, across counties present in both years. Computed from 2010 onward to avoid the Census occupation coding change."
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

wide_2010=df[df["year"]==2010].set_index("county_fips")
wide_2023=df[df["year"]==2023].set_index("county_fips")
common=wide_2010.index.intersection(wide_2023.index)

rank_rows=[]
for col, name in area_names.items():
    rho=spearmanr(wide_2010.loc[common, col], wide_2023.loc[common, col]).statistic
    rank_rows.append({"Task group":name, "Rank correlation, 2010 to 2023":rho})
rankcorr_df=pd.DataFrame(rank_rows)

(GT(rankcorr_df)
  .fmt_number(columns="Rank correlation, 2010 to 2023", decimals=2)
  .cols_align(align="right", columns="Rank correlation, 2010 to 2023")
  .tab_source_note("Spearman correlation across counties present in both years."))
```

Finally, the coefficients themselves hold across time. @tbl-stability refits the level panel regression on the pre pandemic window, 2010 to 2019, and the post pandemic window, 2021 to 2023, the same windows named in @sec-analysis. These are level coefficients in raw dollars, so they run larger than the \$846 reported above from the log specification at the panel mean. The task group ordering is identical in both windows and in the full panel, and the magnitudes move modestly, so the association is not an artifact of any one period, recession, recovery, or pandemic era.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stability
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Level panel regression task group coefficients, in dollars per one percentage point shift, refit on the pre pandemic and post pandemic windows alongside the full panel. Standard errors clustered by county in every fit."

def fit_window(frame):
    Xw=pd.concat([frame[res_cols],
                  pd.get_dummies(frame["year"], prefix="year", drop_first=True).astype(float)], axis=1)
    Xw=sm.add_constant(Xw)
    return sm.OLS(frame["affordability_salary"], Xw).fit(
        cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": frame["county_fips"]})

windows={"Full panel": reg,
         "2010 to 2019": reg[(reg["year"]>=2010)&(reg["year"]<=2019)],
         "2021 to 2023": reg[reg["year"]>=2021]}

stab_rows=[]
for term, name in zip(group_terms, group_names):
    row={"Task group":name}
    for wname, frame in windows.items():
        row[wname]=fit_window(frame).params[term]/100
    stab_rows.append(row)
stability_df=pd.DataFrame(stab_rows)

(GT(stability_df)
  .fmt_currency(columns=["Full panel","2010 to 2019","2021 to 2023"], decimals=0)
  .tab_source_note("Dollars per one percentage point shift out of non-routine cognitive work."))
```

Together, the stability of the national picture, of the county orderings, and of the coefficients supports reading the headline association as a durable characteristic of local economies. The counties whose work is most routine and most manual entered the study period with less purchasing power, and fifteen years later they largely still do. What this means, what it cannot mean, and where it points next are taken up in @sec-conclusions.
